meta.title: Who really said "A free people ought not only to be armed and disciplined, but they should have sufficient arms and ammunition to maintain a status of independence from any who might attempt to abuse them"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No. Only the first phrase is Washington's (8 Jan 1790); the rest was added by W. Cleon Skousen in 1975 and later mis-credited to him.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A free people ought not only to be armed and disciplined, but they should have sufficient arms and ammunition to maintain a status of independence from any who might attempt to abuse them'?
meta.ogDescription: A fabricated conflation: Washington's authentic 1790 line about domestic arms manufacturing was expanded with anti-government language in 1975.

answer.label: Not George Washington — a 1975 conflation
answer.authorDates: 1732–1799 · First U.S. President & Commander-in-Chief of the Continental Army
answer.sourceLine: Only the opening ten words are genuinely Washington’s, from his First Annual Message to Congress on 8 January 1790, where he urged domestic manufacture of “military supplies.” The tail — “sufficient arms and ammunition to maintain a status of independence from any who might attempt to abuse them” — was not written by Washington; per Quote Investigator it was added by author W. Cleon Skousen in 1975 and later mis-credited to Washington.

source.heading: What Washington actually said
source.excerpt: A free people ought not only to be armed but disciplined; to which end a uniform and well digested plan is requisite: And their safety and interest require that they should promote such manufactories, as tend to render them independent on others, for essential, particularly for military supplies.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the full quote to a 1975 blend of Washington’s real 1790 words with commentary by author W. Cleon Skousen, later mistaken for Washington’s own.
The genuine line appears in Washington’s First Annual Message to Congress and concerns promoting domestic “manufactories” of military supplies, not resistance to government.
PolitiFact rated the meme version “Mostly False,” noting the added “sufficient arms and ammunition” language is not Washington’s.
The editors of the Washington Papers confirm the authentic 1790 wording and its manufacturing context.
source.excerptNote: Washington’s authentic sentence, from his 8 January 1790 address. The popular quote keeps only the first phrase and replaces the rest — about domestic weapons manufacturing — with a fabricated passage about arming against “any who might attempt to abuse them.”

sourceLink.text: Washington’s First Annual Message (8 Jan 1790), Avalon Project

source.rightsNote: The quote as circulated is a fabricated hybrid, so no clean copyright status attaches to it. Washington’s authentic 1790 sentence is long in the public domain; the added “sufficient arms and ammunition…abuse them” language originated in 1975 editorial commentary and is not Washington’s work — we assert no public-domain status for the composite.

author.name: George Washington
author.heading: About George Washington
author.bio: George Washington (1732–1799) led the Continental Army through the American Revolution and served as the first President of the United States from 1789 to 1797. In his First Annual Message to Congress on 8 January 1790 — the first State of the Union — he urged the young nation to build its own arms manufacturing so it would not depend on foreigners for military supplies, a lesson drawn from the Continental Army’s wartime shortages. That passage, not any call for citizens to arm against their own government, is the true root of this quote.

misattribution.heading: How the fake grew from the real
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared spurious Washington gun quotes. Its first ten words are authentic; everything after is a modern addition that reverses Washington’s actual point.

items.why: Washington never wrote “sufficient arms and ammunition to maintain a status of independence from any who might attempt to abuse them.” Quote Investigator and PolitiFact both find only the opening phrase is genuine.

Per Quote Investigator, author W. Cleon Skousen combined Washington’s 1790 line with his own commentary in 1975; readers later dropped the seam and credited the whole thing to Washington — the phrase “which would include their own government” is often appended in newer versions.

misattribution.truthLine: Washington’s real 1790 sentence argued for domestic manufacture of military supplies so the nation would be “independent on others” — not for citizens arming against their own government, as the original text makes plain.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The quote is routinely deployed in Second Amendment debates as if Washington endorsed an armed citizenry as a check on government. The authentic 1790 passage does the opposite kind of work: it is a plea for the fledgling United States to build its own arsenals and powder mills so it would not have to buy “military supplies” from foreign powers — a supply-chain argument born of the Continental Army’s wartime shortages.

The fabricated tail, traced to 1975, grafts a distinctly modern anti-tyranny reading onto a founder who, as president, actually led troops to put down the Whiskey Rebellion. That gap between the real sentence and the meme is exactly why it keeps getting fact-checked.
context.pull: Authentic in its first ten words; fabricated in everything that makes it quotable.
